summary: Gives an overview of the design space for reliable multicast of bulk data and describes how application constraints affect possible solutions. It is an informational memo.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending one copy of data to many receivers over IP is called multicast, and making it reliable is a different problem in every application. RFC 2887 maps out the options: what receivers confirm, how missing packets are repaired, and how the sender keeps the network from becoming congested. It ends by arguing for standardising the pieces rather than whole protocols.

questions: how to reliably multicast bulk data
how do multicast congestion control mechanisms work
what is the reliable multicast design space
subtitle: The options for reliable multicast, and how an application's needs narrow them down

tldr.problem: There is no general purpose reliable multicast protocol, because different applications need different things from it, and the requirements of an application cut the design space down sharply.
tldr.mechanism: The memo maps the space: what receivers confirm and at what level, whether differences between receivers must be constrained, how the loss is repaired with acknowledgements, negative acknowledgements, replication or forward error correction, and how the sender keeps the network from becoming congested.
tldr.outcome: The conclusion for standardizers is that whole reliable multicast protocols should not be standardized in one pass. They should be broken into functional building blocks and standardized separately, so that new applications can reuse tested mechanisms.

today: RFC 2887 is an Informational memo that has not been obsoleted or updated. It is a survey rather than a specification, and its advice to standardizers is to build reliable multicast out of separable pieces rather than to standardise a whole transport protocol in one pass.

sections.title: No One Reliable Multicast Protocol Fits All
sections.content:
The memo opens by calling the phrase general purpose reliable multicast protocol something of an oxymoron. Different applications have different requirements of a reliable multicast protocol, and those requirements cut the design space down in ways that two applications with different needs often cannot share a single solution. Many successful designs, though, serve more special purpose requirements well.

The review covers reliable multicast protocols intended for bulk data transfer, a term taken to have broad meaning: the main limitations are that the data stream is continuous and long-lived, and that the constraints necessary for the forms of congestion control we understand are present. The purpose is to gather an overview of the field and make explicit the constraints imposed by particular mechanisms, and to give guidance to the standardization process for protocols and protocol building blocks. Potential solutions are clustered into loose categories, and real protocols may be composed of mechanisms from more than one of them.

The main constraint on any solution is the need to scale to large receiver sets; for small receiver sets the design space is much less restricted. The conclusion repeats the point in a form aimed at standardizers: because application requirements constrain the solutions so tightly and the applications are so diverse, any standardization work should take great pains to be future-proof. That seems to imply not standardizing complete reliable multicast transport protocols in one pass, but rather examining the degree to which such protocols can be separated into functional building blocks and standardizing those blocks separately as far as that makes sense. That approach allows protocol evolution and lets applications with new constraints reuse existing, tested mechanisms.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no such thing as a reliable multicast protocol that suits everything. A stock price feed needs every receiver to see the same data at the same time; a file download needs every byte; a radio broadcast can lose a packet or two. RFC 2887 sorts the options and explains what each one costs, and asks standardizers to build the pieces rather than a single whole protocol.

sections.title: What the Application Needs
sections.content:
The requirements an application brings are as broad as the applications themselves, but the memo lists a set that significantly affect the design of a protocol: whether the application needs to know that everyone received the data; whether it needs to constrain differences between receivers; whether it needs to scale to large numbers of receivers; whether it needs to be totally reliable; whether it needs ordered data; whether it needs low-delay delivery; whether it needs time-bounded delivery; whether it needs many interacting senders; whether the data flow is intermittent; whether it needs to work in the public Internet; whether it needs to work without a return path, as with satellite; and whether it needs secure delivery. For bulk data transfer standards, two of these are ruled out: applications with multiple interacting senders and intermittent data flows are set aside, not because they are unimportant but because there is not yet effective congestion control for them.

Several definitions follow. An application data unit is a logically separable unit of data that is useful to the application, and it may be short enough to fit in a single packet, such as an event notification or a stock quote, or much longer, such as a software package. A protocol may optionally provide delivery confirmation in two forms. Application data unit confirmation tells the application about receiver progress and when to stop sending packets about a particular unit; packet confirmation tells the transport layer when it can release buffer space. An application that needs to know that every receiver got the unit, or which receivers failed to get all of it, needs a positive acknowledgement from every receiver, although these may be aggregated, and needing to know precisely which receivers failed puts extra constraints on that aggregation. Different mechanisms can serve the two levels in the same application: an ADU-level confirmation using positive acknowledgements may sit on top of a packet-level NACK or FEC-based transport, which typically makes sense only when ADUs are much larger than a packet.

Three further requirements shape the design. Constraining differences between receivers, so that all receivers stay within some range, is hard to satisfy without harming performance; the usual solution is not to send more than a limited amount of new data until positive acknowledgements arrive from everyone, which copes badly with network and end-system failures. Receiver set scaling is the most important constraint, because a protocol must get good throughput of application data units and provide good congestion control, and scaling strictly limits the mechanisms available; the memo walks through flat acknowledgements, aggregate acknowledgements, NACKs, ACK trees and rings, and open-loop FEC encodings that scale to an infinite number of receivers because they use no feedback channel at all. Some applications need total reliability, since a missing part of an application data unit makes the received part useless, as with file transfer; others, such as audio broadcasting, can lose packets and still be usable, so a semi-reliable protocol is often enough. Time-bounded delivery applies where late data is worthless, as with real-time audio or video or where new data supersedes old; it usually implies a semi-reliable protocol, though the converse does not hold.
sections.plainLanguage: What the application needs decides everything else. Does it have to know that every receiver got the file? Does it mind if one receiver is a second behind the others? How many receivers are there? Is a lost packet fatal, or does the next one cover for it? Is late data worthless? The memo runs through these questions and shows how each one rules mechanisms in or out.

sections.title: What the Network Allows
sections.content:
The network the application is deployed in constrains the design space too. In principle the Internet and an intranet are the same, but in practice an intranet is under one administration and may allow solutions that cannot easily be done in the public Internet. If the data is of very high value, it might be appropriate to enhance the routers to help a reliable multicast transport protocol; in the public Internet the extra expense of supporting that state in routers is less likely to be acceptable.

Feedback is the other constraint. Feedback from receivers can be multicast or unicast. Multicast feedback has advantages, especially in NACK-based protocols where it is valuable for NACK suppression, but it is not clear that all providers will let every member of a session send to that session; if multicast feedback is not allowed, unicast feedback can almost always be substituted, at the cost of extra messages and mechanisms. Some networks allow no feedback at all, the prime example being satellite broadcast where the back channel may be very narrow or non-existent; for those networks only FEC-based encodings have any real chance of working. If the receivers are direct satellite receivers no congestion control is needed, but it is dangerous to make that assumption, because a satellite hop may feed downstream networks, so congestion control still has to be considered in solutions without a return path.

Finally, the memo clusters protocols into four classes by how much help they get from other network elements. With no additional support the routers merely forward packets, and only the sender and receivers hold protocol state. In layered approaches the data is split across multiple multicast groups and receivers join the groups they need, which may require fast join and leave from the routers and more forwarding state there. In server-based approaches extra nodes help with delivery or aggregate feedback; they need not be senders or receivers and may exist only on the distribution or feedback tree. In router-based approaches the routers on the normal distribution tree help with delivery or with feedback aggregation and suppression; they have more control over which traffic reaches which members, but routers have little spare memory or processing power, and router code is harder to upgrade than application code, so such approaches must be very general.
sections.plainLanguage: Where the data travels matters too. Inside a network that one organisation runs, the operators can change the routers to help; on the public Internet that is much less likely. Feedback from receivers can be multicast or sent one to one, and some networks allow no feedback at all, as with satellite, where only the redundancy-coding approach has a chance. The memo sorts protocols by how much help they expect from the network: none, groups, extra servers or the routers themselves.

sections.title: Mechanisms for Repairing Loss
sections.content:
Two concerns drive the design: congestion control and good throughput. Packet loss plays a major role in both, since the primary symptom of congestion in many networks is packet loss and the primary obstacle to good throughput is also packet loss, so measuring and reacting to loss is crucial. The memo groups the mechanisms into three families: data packet acknowledgment, negative acknowledgment of missing data packets, and redundancy that allows not all packets to be received.

The simplest ACK-based scheme has every receiver acknowledge every data packet and the sender resend what any receiver lost, which is limited to very small receiver groups by the implosion of acknowledgements at the sender. Putting several acknowledgements into one packet reduces the implosion by a constant amount and allows slightly larger groups, but soon the feedback becomes too infrequent for sender-based congestion control to work reliably. Arranging receivers in a ring, with an acknowledgement token passed around, prevents the implosion, but ring creation and maintenance may be problematic, and a ring that ignores network topology can make the number of acknowledgement packets crossing the backbone grow in proportion to the number of receivers.

Tree-based acknowledgement is described as more robust and more easily configured than a ring. Receivers send acknowledgements to a parent node, which aggregates them and passes them on up the tree, while data is still multicast from the sender as normal. Trees are easier to construct because more local information can be used, and they can be more fault tolerant because a node failure affects only a subset of receivers, each of which can locally decide to bypass its parent and report to the node one level higher. With good tree formation this is potentially one of the most scalable solutions. To be easy to deploy, tree-based protocols must be self-organising, and the scaling limits then come from tree formation and maintenance rather than from the acknowledgements themselves; without a scalable automatic mechanism, tree-based protocols need manual configuration, which limits them, often to intranets. Subtree retransmission is a separate issue: with the right router mechanisms or several multicast groups, intermediate tree nodes could retransmit missing data to the nodes below them instead of the original sender doing it, but that needs good correlation between the ACK tree and the real data tree and a way to constrain the retransmission to the subtree. Interior nodes can aggregate in three ways: sending one acknowledgement when all their children have acknowledged, listing the children that have acknowledged, or sending an aggregated acknowledgement with a NACK-like exception list. The first is the most scalable for data packets, while the second and third tell the sender exactly who received it; doing the first per packet and the third per application data unit is the most scalable combination for applications that need that detail.

NACK-based mechanisms send a negative acknowledgement only for packets a receiver discovers it did not receive, which has advantages: the sender no longer needs to know how many receivers there are, so no topology-building phase is needed for ring or tree schemes; fault tolerance is simpler because receivers are responsible for reliability; sender state shrinks because the sender does not track receiver state; and a single NACK can stand for a packet missing at any number of receivers, so NACK suppression is possible. The disadvantages are that the sender has a harder time knowing when it can free transmission buffers, and that extra session-level machinery is needed if the sender really must know whether a particular receiver received everything. The difference between NACK-based protocols lies mostly in how suppression is done. SRM uses random timers weighted by the round trip time to each node missing the data, which needs the round trip time computed before suppression works properly. NTE uses a sender-triggered mechanism based on random keys and sliding masks, needs no random timers and works for very large sessions, but makes it hard to provide the constant low-level feedback that congestion control needs. AAP uses exponentially distributed random timers and is effective for large sessions without computing round trip times. PGM and LMS add router mechanisms to suppress duplicate NACKs, with PGM supplementing SRM-style timers and localising the suppression. The memo judges exponentially weighted random timers the most general, because SRM-style timers are harder to use correctly when round trip times or the number of responders are unknown.

Two mechanisms avoid per-packet repair. Replication designs the stream so that no explicit reliability is needed except in rare cases: a multicast game can multicast the position of a moving object continuously, because a new position supersedes the old one before any retransmission could take place, but an explicit mechanism is needed when the object interacts with others or stops moving; the shared text editor works the same way by sending the whole changed line. The advantage is that replication is not susceptible to spatially uncorrelated packet loss, and the traffic does not grow as the receiver group grows. Forward error correction, in the form of erasure codes, is the other. The simplest form XORs a group of packets together to form a new packet that is also sent, so a receiver missing one original packet but holding the XOR packet can reproduce it; more general codes generate n encoding packets from k original data packets, and receiving any k of the n encoding packets reproduces the originals. The sender groups data into rounds, and a round may be an entire application data unit or a small part of one. Erasure codes beat simple retransmission because the dependency on which packets were lost is removed, so repair traffic for spatially uncorrelated loss falls considerably. Schemes divide into proactive, where the sender decides in advance how many encoding packets to send per round, and reactive, where the sender sends only the original data at first and then uses feedback to work out how many packets the worst-hit receiver lost, sending that many extra encoding packets, which then also repair the smaller losses elsewhere. FEC reduces repair traffic well but requires the data to be grouped into rounds, which can add end-to-end latency; for bulk data that is usually not a problem, but for interactive applications replication may be better.
sections.plainLanguage: Five ways of coping with a lost packet are compared. Every receiver can confirm every packet, but the replies flood the sender. Receivers can confirm to a parent that passes the confirmations up a tree, which scales but needs the tree built and kept. Receivers can instead report only the packets they missed, which is quieter but needs the repeats suppressed. A stream can repeat itself so that a new value replaces an old one. Or the sender can send extra coded packets from which a missing one can be rebuilt.

sections.title: Congestion Control Choices
sections.content:
The basic delivery model of the Internet is best-effort, with no guarantees of throughput, delay or loss, so end systems are expected to be adaptive and to reduce their transmission rate to match the congestion state of the network. Even where the Internet starts to support reserved bandwidth and differentiated service classes, an end system that has not explicitly reserved bandwidth must still perform congestion control.

The memo sets out five classes of single-sender multicast congestion control. In the sender-controlled, one group scheme a single multicast group carries the data and feedback from the group members controls the rate of that group, with the goal of transmitting at a rate dictated by the slowest receiver. Sender-controlled with multiple groups starts from one group that is adaptively subdivided into subgroups centred on congestion points; application-level relays buffer data from a group nearer the sender and retransmit it more slowly into a group further away, so different receivers receive the data at different rates, and the sender-based control happens between the members of a subgroup and their relay. In the receiver-controlled, one group scheme the receivers decide for themselves whether the sender is transmitting too fast for the current congestion state and leave the group if it is. Receiver-controlled with a layered organisation stripes data across several groups and has receivers join and leave those groups according to their own measurements, so that the amount of data received stays right; it relies on receivers behind the same bottleneck joining and leaving in a coordinated fashion, and the memo says it has not been completely confirmed that this will scale in practice. Router-based control adds mechanisms to multicast routers: conditional joins, where a join states a loss rate above which the router may refuse it; filtering of traffic that exceeds a reasonable rate, possibly at different rates in different places; and fair queuing combined with end-to-end adaptation. Router-based schemes need more state in backbone routers than has traditionally been acceptable, so in the near term they are likely to apply only to intranets.

For reliable multicast, congestion control has to be considered at the same time as reliability, and the same mechanisms are sometimes used for both. Where the control is receiver-based, open-loop delivery using FEC is the likely choice for good throughput in bulk transfer, because open-loop delivery needs no feedback and so matches a receiver-based scheme that works without feedback.
sections.plainLanguage: The Internet gives no guarantees, so the sender has to slow down when the network is busy. There are five ways to arrange that. The sender can watch the replies and pace itself, either in one group or in several groups split around busy points. The receivers can watch and leave the group when the data arrives too fast. Or the routers can help, by refusing a join that expects too much loss or by dropping traffic that arrives too quickly. Router help needs more memory in backbone routers, so it is mainly an intranet option.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Security has relatively little effect on the design space for reliable multicast protocols. The primary issues constraining the space are all related to receiver-set scaling. For authentication of the source and for data integrity, scaling is not a significant issue, but data encryption, key distribution and especially re-keying may be significantly affected by it; tree and graph based re-keying would appear to be appropriate solutions, though it is not clear that they need to affect the design of the data distribution part of the protocol.

The main question for security is the role of third parties. If nodes other than the original source are allowed to send or resend data packets, the security model has to take that into account, and in particular it must be clear whether such third parties are trusted or untrusted; a requirement for trusted third parties can make protocols hard to deploy on the Internet. Untrusted third parties, such as receivers that retransmit data, may be used so long as the authentication mechanisms account for it, which typically means the original sender digitally signs and timestamps the data and the third parties resend that signed, timestamped payload unmodified.

Denial of service attacks on multicast transport state are easy if the design does not account for them, because any receiver can join the session and then produce feedback that influences the progress of a session involving many other receivers. A receiver that asks for retransmission of every packet, or that refuses to acknowledge packets in an ACK-based protocol, can bring a session to a standstill, so senders need policy for such conditions and may have to evict the receiver from the group. A single receiver masquerading as a large number of receivers may still be an issue with protocols that support NACK-like functionality, and giving each NACKer a unique key when it first sends a NACK, with a unicast response, might prevent that. Flooding attacks are easier to protect against than with unicast, because unwanted senders can be pruned from the distribution tree using the mechanisms in IGMP version 3.
sections.plainLanguage: Security barely narrows the choices here; scaling does. Encrypting the data and, above all, changing the keys later are both harder when there are many receivers, so tree-shaped and graph-shaped key management are suggested. The bigger question is whether anyone other than the original sender may resend data, and if so whether they are trusted. And because any receiver can join and then send misleading feedback, a single receiver can stall the whole session unless the sender has a way to eject it.

items.title: Sender-controlled, one group
items.text: Feedback from the group sets the rate, so the slowest receiver dictates the speed.

items.title: Sender-controlled, multiple groups
items.text: The group is split around congestion points and relays resend more slowly further out.

items.title: Receiver-controlled, one group
items.text: Receivers leave the group when the sender is going too fast for the network.

items.title: Receiver-controlled, layered
items.text: Receivers join and leave groups to match their own measurement of congestion.

items.title: Router-based
items.text: Routers refuse joins with too high a loss rate, filter excess traffic, or queue fairly.
